description: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs, speed, velocity, acceleration, and terminal velocity.
content_html:
Speed and Velocity

Speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation linking distance, speed and time is:

$$s = v \times t$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m), \(v\) is speed (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). You can rearrange this to find speed (\(v = \frac{s}{t}\)) or time (\(t = \frac{s}{v}\)). Typical speeds to know: walking (~1.5 m/s), running (~3 m/s), cycling (~6 m/s), a car in town (~13 m/s), and the speed of sound in air (~340 m/s).

Velocity is speed in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity. An object travelling in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction constantly changes — meaning it is always accelerating, even though its speed stays the same.

Similarly, distance (scalar) measures total ground covered, while displacement (vector) measures how far and in what direction from the start. A runner completing a 400 m lap of a track covers a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of zero — they end up back where they started.

Key Fact

Speed and distance are scalars (magnitude only). Velocity and displacement are vectors (magnitude + direction). An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because direction constantly changes.

Acceleration

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration (m/s²), \(v\) is final velocity (m/s), \(u\) is initial velocity (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). A negative value means the object is decelerating. For example, a car braking from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s has an acceleration of \(a = \frac{0 - 20}{5} = -4 \text{ m/s}^2\).

Question: A cyclist accelerates from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate her acceleration.

Step 1: Identify values: \(u = 2 \text{ m/s}\), \(v = 14 \text{ m/s}\), \(t = 6 \text{ s}\).

Step 2: Apply the equation: \(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{14 - 2}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ m/s}^2\)

Note: Always include units in your final answer. Forgetting units is one of the most common reasons for losing marks on calculation questions.

Distance-Time Graphs

On a distance-time graph, time is always plotted on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed. You can read the shape of the line as follows:

• A horizontal line means the object is stationary (speed = 0).
• A straight diagonal line means constant speed — steeper gradient means greater speed.
• A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating.
• A curve getting shallower means the object is decelerating.

To find the speed at a specific instant on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate its gradient.

Key Fact

On a distance-time graph: gradient = speed. On a velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration. Time is always on the x-axis for motion graphs. Plotting them the wrong way round is a common exam error.

Velocity-Time Graphs

On a velocity-time graph, two key pieces of information can be extracted:

• The gradient equals the acceleration. A steeper slope means greater acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration). A downward slope means deceleration.
• A line below the x-axis means the object is moving in the opposite direction.

The area under the line on a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled. For a triangle, the area is \(\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\). For a rectangle, it is base × height. For irregular shapes, split into triangles and rectangles and add them together.

To measure the speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp, mark a measured distance on the ramp. Use a stopwatch to time how long the trolley takes to travel between two marked points, then calculate speed using \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). For greater precision, use light gates connected to a data logger — these measure very short time intervals as the trolley interrupts the beam, allowing you to calculate instantaneous speed. Using two light gates at different positions lets you compare speeds and calculate acceleration.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (such as air or water), two forces act on it: its weight (downwards) and drag (upwards, opposing motion). Initially, weight is much greater than drag, so the object accelerates downwards. As speed increases, drag increases. Eventually, drag equals weight. At this point the resultant force is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.

A skydiver provides a clear example. After jumping, they accelerate rapidly. As speed builds, air resistance increases until it equals their weight — this is their first terminal velocity (around 55 m/s for a spread-eagled position). When the parachute opens, surface area dramatically increases, causing air resistance to suddenly far exceed weight. The skydiver decelerates until a new, much lower terminal velocity is reached (around 5–7 m/s), safe for landing.

On a velocity-time graph, terminal velocity appears as a curve that starts steep (rapid acceleration) and gradually flattens out to a horizontal line (constant velocity). The curve of a parachute opening would show a sharp decrease in velocity before levelling off again at the lower terminal speed.
exam_tip_html: For motion graph questions, always label your axes with both the quantity and the unit (e.g. “time / s”, “velocity / m/s”) — missing units on axes costs marks. Time must always go on the x-axis for motion graphs. When asked to “describe the motion”, refer to the gradient explicitly: “the gradient is decreasing, so the object is decelerating.” For extended responses on terminal velocity, make sure you state that the resultant force is zero, not just that “forces are equal” — the command word “explain” requires the link between zero resultant force and zero acceleration.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed and distance are scalars; velocity and displacement are vectors. Acceleration = rate of change of velocity, calculated using \(a = \frac{v-u}{t}\). Always include units in your answer.
  • On a distance-time graph, gradient = speed (time on x-axis always). On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration; area under line = distance. Horizontal line = constant velocity (not necessarily stationary).
  • Terminal velocity is reached when drag equals weight (resultant force = zero, acceleration = zero). A parachute increases drag, producing a lower second terminal velocity safe for landing.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a vector quantity?
A) Speed
B) Distance
C) Mass
D) Velocity
practice_questions.marks:
D) Velocity [1 mark]
Velocity has both magnitude and direction, making it a vector. Speed, distance and mass are all scalars.

practice_questions.text: State the equation used to calculate acceleration from initial velocity, final velocity, and time.
practice_questions.marks:
\(a = \frac{v - u}{t}\) [1 mark]
Where a = acceleration (m/s²), v = final velocity (m/s), u = initial velocity (m/s), t = time (s).

practice_questions.text: A car travels at a constant speed of 18 m/s and then brakes, coming to rest in 9 seconds. Calculate the deceleration of the car. Give your answer in m/s².
practice_questions.marks:
Identify values: u = 18 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 9 s [1 mark]
Apply equation: a = (v − u) ÷ t [1 mark]
a = (0 − 18) ÷ 9 = −2 m/s² [1 mark]
Deceleration = 2 m/s² (accept −2 m/s²; award final mark for correct unit) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A distance-time graph shows a straight line with a positive gradient, followed by a horizontal section, and then a steeper straight line with a positive gradient.
Describe the motion of the object during each section.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three sections described accurately — constant speed (gradient = speed), stationary (horizontal = zero speed), then faster constant speed (steeper gradient = greater speed). [2 marks]
Secure: Two sections described correctly. [2 marks]
Developing: One section described correctly. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague reference to motion with no use of gradient. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what happens to the acceleration and velocity of a skydiver from the moment they jump to when they reach terminal velocity. Refer to the forces acting on the skydiver.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies weight > air resistance initially → resultant force downwards → acceleration. As speed increases, air resistance increases. When air resistance = weight, resultant force = zero, acceleration = zero, terminal velocity reached. Correct direction of all forces stated. [3 marks]
Secure: States weight and air resistance, mentions resultant force = zero at terminal velocity, some description of changing acceleration. [2 marks]
Developing: Mentions two forces but does not explain how they change or link to resultant force. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague — 'forces balance' without explanation. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student plots a velocity-time graph for a ball rolling down a slope and then across a flat surface. The ball reaches the flat surface after 4 seconds with a velocity of 8 m/s, and its velocity stays constant for a further 6 seconds.
Calculate the total distance travelled by the ball in this 10-second journey. You must show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Distance on slope (0–4 s): area of triangle = ½ × 4 × 8 = 16 m [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Distance on flat (4–10 s): area of rectangle = 6 × 8 = 48 m [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Total distance = 16 + 48 = 64 m [1 mark]
Unit stated (m) [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct method and answer with units and clear working.
Secure: Correct method for both sections, minor arithmetic error.
Developing: Correct method for one section only.
Emerging: Attempts to use distance = speed × time but does not split into sections.

knowledge_checks.q: On a distance-time graph, what does the gradient of the line represent?
A skydiver reaches terminal velocity when which condition is met?
options: Weight is greater than air resistance
Air resistance is greater than weight
Air resistance equals weight so resultant force is zero
The skydiver stops accelerating because there is no air resistance

knowledge_checks.q: Velocity is speed in a stated _____. It is a vector quantity.
On a velocity-time graph, _____ is always plotted on the x-axis.
Match each graph feature to what it represents:
left: Horizontal line on a velocity-time graph

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
flashcard_questions.a: Speed is a scalar (magnitude only); velocity is a vector (magnitude + direction).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
What equation links acceleration, final velocity, initial velocity and time?
What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph indicate?
What does a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph indicate?

flashcard_questions.a: The constant speed reached when drag equals weight, giving zero resultant force.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a falling object accelerate at first?
flashcard_questions.a: Weight is greater than air resistance, so there is a downward resultant force.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to a skydiver's speed when they open their parachute?
flashcard_questions.a: They decelerate — increased surface area causes drag to exceed weight.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two examples of vector quantities.
A runner completes a 400 m lap and returns to the start. What is their displacement?
flashcard_questions.a: Zero — they end at the same point they started.

glossary_terms.definition: The distance travelled per unit time, measured in metres per second (m/s). Speed is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction.
Speed in a given direction. Velocity is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction.
The shortest straight-line distance from start to finish, measured in a specific direction. Displacement is a vector.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s². Acceleration is a vector quantity.
A graph with time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. The gradient of the line gives the speed of the object.
A graph with time on the x-axis and velocity on the y-axis. The gradient gives acceleration and the area under the line gives distance travelled.
A straight line that touches a curve at exactly one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The constant speed reached by a falling object when the upward drag force equals the downward weight, giving zero resultant force and zero acceleration.
